utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next witness is Mr. Ivo Mrso who rounds out our Bugojno evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, would you please state your full name for the Court?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Ivo Mrso.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, I would like to take you, very quickly, through some preliminary matters regarding your personal background. I believe that you were born on March 20th, 1938 in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You are a Croat and a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you are presently divorced and have two daughters.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that you completed your secondary school education in Bugojno and then in 1965 graduated from Zagreb University Agricultural School?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You worked in the north of Bosnia-Herzegovina for about nine years as an agricultural engineer then returned to Bugojno first to work as the manager of an agricultural manufacturing company and then working as a manager of a mill in which position you remained until the Muslim attack in Bugojno on July 18th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that you stayed throughout the civil war in Bugojno and that during the hostilities, you lost your mother, brother, and sister-in-law who were killed by Muslim forces during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then during the occupation of the town by Muslim forces in 1993 and 1994 you essentially acted as the representative or the spokesman for the few remaining Croats in the area.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In April of 1997, sir, I believe that you were appointed to be Assistant Minister of Agriculture for the District of Central Bosnia in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Currently you are the president of the Bugojno Municipal Council which is the legislative branch of the municipal government?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I believe, sir, since 1990, you have been a member of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina and since 1995 you have held the position of vice-president of the Bugojno branch of that political party?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, we've heard, as you will appreciate, a lot of evidence in this case concerning preliminary matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Might I just inquire of the Court whether it wishes us to go over paragraph 6 or can we simply have that essentially taken as read and move on to the more salient portions of Mr. Mrso's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you'd like to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that turning to paragraph 7 of the outline that you signed on Saturday, when the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, and the Bosnian Serb army, the BSA, attacked Bugojno towards the end of May of 1992 it was the HVO that essentially defended the town?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you recount in your statement a meeting held between members of the HVO and the Territorial Defence in August of 1992. Could you tell us a little bit about that, please?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: This was not just a meeting of the representatives, but other prominent citizens of Bugojno also attended it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And could you tell us a little bit about the meeting, what was discussed, whether any agreements were reached and if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: For the most part, the issue of Muslim refugees was discussed, that is, the refugees who arrived in Bugojno from other areas where they were driven out by the Serbs. Also, there was other topics which were also discussed, especially the economic situation, because Bugojno was enclosed and the economic situation was very difficult, and the second part of the meeting was devoted to discussing the defence because on the 24th of May, the Serbs had started shelling Bugojno and the situation in the town was not satisfactory at all. I personally advocated that Muslims and Croats should reach more agreements because of the threat of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And what was the upshot or the eventual result of these discussions regarding a joint defence of Bugojno between HVO forces and TO forces, Mr. Mrso?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Not much was said in this meeting about that. Only in the utterances, that is, the discussions of various people. It turned out that there was some disagreements there which was a bit surprising, and I think that took us by surprise. For instance, a Muslim representative openly stated that the defence positions should be separated and that the Muslims should keep their own and the Croats their own sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did the Muslim representatives in these discussions regarding a potential joint defence show much interest in the idea of establishing a joint defence of the town, in your view?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Through my activities in Bugojno in my party and overall, I realised that they were not considered very important. They were a bit passive and I remember personally when the people, the Muslims came from Donji Vakuf when I was in the party office. For instance, about 15 Muslims came from Donji Vakuf and they came to me, and I called the SDA secretary and directed them there. After a while they came back to me, they came back and they said that they had not been given any answers there, that they were willing to join in, to participant, that they would join the HDZ. And through that, they wanted arms. As an official on duty, I couldn't take such decisions on my own, and then -- so I could not give them the right answer and I don't know who gave them, if anybody did, the right answer later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Just a few details surrounding the ethnic make-up of Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Your Honours, if I could just draw the Court's attention to volume 22 of the Kordic trial exhibits filed last Monday. That's a copy of the official census.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that according to the census, the municipality of Bugojno had a total population of some 46.889 people, 19.697 of whom were Muslims, 16.031 being Croats, 8.673 being Serbs, and also about 2.500 Yugoslavs and others. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you describe in your outline that while the HVO was fighting on the front lines with the JNA and BSA, ABiH troops were gathering in town and that there were problems caused by a large influx of Muslim refugees. Could you just describe for the Court the progress of events in Bugojno and the problems caused by the influx of refugees, concentrating specifically, if you would, upon the effects upon the Croat population in the town, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I have said that there were many refugees there. And personally, I considered, because Bugojno was at the front line, that something should be done, because there were too many refugees and it created economic problems and other problems. In addition, I was in charge of the state reserves at the republican and municipal levels, and everybody wanted them: flour, sugar, cooking oil, and so on. The Serbs had cheated us out of some of these reserves, and I realised that there was a problem, and the Muslims had no answer to that. I met with people from their logistics, because they were always asking for flour, and I said that the situation was untenable, that people should be moved on behind the front lines, and also that their security should be taken into consideration. But I noticed that they were keeping the active-duty personnel. There were Muslims who were already smuggling arms. And there was part -- in the part of the defence line where the Croats were deployed, we did not have enough weapons, so we wanted to somehow get weapons to these people. And I said that we could find a deal, that we could swap arms for other things. And I found it strange that people were not really discussing the joint defence very much, and that was all surprising to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you have an estimate, Mr. Mrso, of the number of Muslim refugees flooding into Bugojno from neighbouring municipalities in this time period?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Officially at that time we operated with the figure of about twelve to thirteen thousand Muslim refugees, mostly from the areas where they were driven out by the Serbs. For instance, all Muslims from Donji Vakuf were in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And could you tell the Court whether there were any incidents of harassment of Croat civilians in late 1992.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. There were some incidents, especially in some areas in the municipality where we tried to set up joint guards. And then there were also incidents in Uskoplje, Gornji Vakuf, and Novi Travnik, because Muslims attacked these people and disarmed them. There was even looting, driving away of cattle, and I have it all down in my journal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were there any murders of Croat civilians, as far as you're aware, and towards the end of 1992 and in early 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. This happened at the border area of Bugojno municipality, towards Uskoplje, Gornji Vakuf, near the road to Novi Travnik -- Bistrica and Novi Travnik. Several Croats from the Travnik area were killed there. I believe that there was also an incident on the road Uskoplje, Gornji Vakuf, Gracanica, Bugojno. They had some secret base or something from where they forayed out at night. I would have to consult my notes for more details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Let me just move on a little bit to paragraph 10, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You talk about the municipality being under constant shelling from BSA artillery, and you also make a reference to Muslims digging trenches in the municipality. Was there anything specific about those trenches that you and your fellow Croat colleagues noticed, Mr. Mrso?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. That was -- that appeared strange to me, because I was in Bugojno, I still worked for the company, I walked on foot. One sort of was careful because of shelling. And every day as I went to work, even before -- in front of buildings in Bugojno, I could see some sandbags and I saw that Muslims started -- had started digging some trenches. All this looked strange to me, and as a local citizen of Bugojno, I asked, "What is going on? Are there any Croats here among them?" And sometimes they were arrogant to me, sometimes those who knew me were more polite to me, but they would just tell me to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Which way were the trenches facing, Mr. Mrso?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: What was strange, for instance, was that at one location was in the village of Porice and the road to Kupres, where Croat soldiers held the defence line, and Muslims were digging trenches and they were facing not towards Kupres, but towards Bugojno. And I pointed that out. I told some people from the HVO about it. Also in the area towards Novi Travnik, on the road to Rostovo, the village of Ljubic, people were saying that the Muslims were taking up positions and beyond them there were positions held by the Croats against the Serbs at Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were there any barricades erected in town or in your own neighbourhood that you saw?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, there were. And there were incidents. There was a Muslim checkpoint. When the Croats would pass, they would take away their cars. And it seemed to me as if it was done intentionally, provoking of these incidents. I remember in 1992, in November --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If counsel wants that sort of detail, Mr. Mrso, he'll ask you. Could you just concentrate on answering the questions which he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcript asks, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you one matter of detail, Mr. Mrso. Do you recall an incident in mid-1992 when Zarko Tole, the HVO commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone at that time was arrested?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Where was he arrested? By whom?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: A meeting was held, a joint meeting with the TO, and after the meeting, after the meeting was over, he, I guess, started back and he was arrested near the municipal building by the Serbs. And the security -- because the chief of the TO at that time was a Muslim, the security was provided by Muslims; and my friend, who was the chief of police in Bugojno at that time, told me afterwards that it must have been Muslims who had set it up, that they had withdrawn the people on duty, and with their nod, Tole was arrested, because he knew about the organisation of defence in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was he handed over essentially to the Serbs by the Muslims as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: That was the story that was current at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let's turn to July 18th, 1993, Mr. Mrso. Could you tell the Court what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: This was the Sunday. As any day, I walked out. I found it a bit strange that very few people were there. I was looking for some newspaper because there was no -- and I got some from a friend. The town was empty. I went home, I read the paper that I got from my friend, and then I noticed in that -- that people were running about in the street. I didn't pay much attention to it. I did not know at all what was going on. Then I went to bed that night. At 3.30 in the morning, somebody started banging at the door. I asked, "Who is it?" They said, "Open up." I asked, "Who is it?" And then there was one burst of fire, another burst of fire. The window -- I went to the floor, then the things quieted down. I dressed up and waited. In the morning, around 7.30, I saw what happened. My front door and everything was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, if I might just interrupt you, sir. The Court has already heard that there was military activity in Bugojno on July the 18th. Who attacked who, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: From what I know now, Muslims attacked, because on that day, Sunday, and I was unaware of this, they rounded up some Croat soldiers from the street. They put them in some houses. They beat them up. Now I know. I later heard that Franjo Jezidzic was detained and beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I don't mean to be impolite, but you will appreciate that we only have a limited time and we have to move forward with the evidence. You've described the incident where Muslim soldiers came to your house, shot out the door and so forth. And I believe that you say in paragraph 11 of your statement that you were put under house arrest with about 10 other Croats in a private house on July 20th, two days after the initial attack. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: That is correct. These were people from my street. We were all brought to one house. The day when they attacked, I was in hiding, and later on I returned to the house thinking it was all over, but then they came for me and took me to a house where I noticed that other neighbours had already been brought there. We could not leave the house, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And subsequently, I believe you were taken to a garage in your neighbourhood and were detained there for another two days along with about 50 other prisoners, both civilian and military.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. Three soldiers arrived in the house where we were detained and called out my name. They had a piece of paper on them. They asked if I was there. I said I was -- they demanded that I go with them. And there, they took me to this garage with another two neighbours. There, I found about 50 other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How big was this garage, sir? Could you just describe the conditions of your detention to the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: The garage was something like five by eight, and the conditions were impossible when I was brought there. In fact, I was kicked inside, and there I found a Muslim who was brandishing a sword or something. He was cursing the people. Everybody had to keep their head between their knees, and they said if anybody looked up, that they would be cut down by a burst of fire. When I was pointed to a place where I could crouch, there was a man half naked with his hands tied behind his back. His mouth was touching the concrete, and I didn't know whether he was alive or dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were there any beatings administered to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: While we were in the garage, the Muslim soldiers would burst in, and at night they would take people out in front of the garage and beat them, and that was horrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You describe one person in your outline, a man by the name of Ivica Keskic. Could you just tell us what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: They kept calling him out. They said, "Keskic, come out." They would then proceed to beat him up. We were horrified. Every time as they kept calling him out, I could not endure this anymore, and I said, "Why doesn't somebody else go out when they call him out because they'll kill him." And a relative of his said, "You're right, I'll do it next time," but then Keskic said that he would not, himself, allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then I believe that you were subsequently moved two days later to an old monastery where you were detained for another ten days.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: It was a convent before, but later on, yes, it became a monastery and they brought us in the morning. We had to board a truck which had canvas and we were all coming on to the truck, and they were shouting, "Faster, faster or I'll cut you down with a burst of fire," and so on and so forth, and they put us in a cellar in the monastery and I counted us, we were some 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You also described an incident, sir, where a Red Cross representative visited the monastery several days later after you had been taken there. Could you tell the Court about that incident, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. I spent two or three days in that cellar, and then I don't know why they took me upstairs to an upper floor where there were another 10 people or so. And one day, representatives, or I believe they were International Red Cross representatives, and our local priest, the parish priest came and a nun and my friend Stjepan Vukadin and a physician. And they were brought in, and the Muslims wouldn't let people talk saying, "Don't you see how well they are?" They would not allow us to talk. These ones here had brought us something to eat, and because there were some people who had been hurt, the physician administered some treatment to them. And to Friar Bruno Batinic, I found a piece of paper and I had written down the names of the people in the cellar and I had it with me upstairs. And since they wouldn't allow us to communicate with these people, nevertheless I managed to pull the priest by the hand and shove this piece of paper into his hand and indicate that they were downstairs; all the others. So the Muslims said, "Well, you can see, there is nobody here, only a few and nobody else arrived," and so on and so forth. And then when one of those who must have come from the International Red Cross -- that they are sure there must be some other people down there and insisted on seeing them, and they refused to. And then they said, "No, we want to see them. We won't leave until we see them." So eventually they did go down to the cellar and saw these 73 men, and yet they were trying to conceal that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were there any beatings administered to the people imprisoned in the monastery of the type that had been administered to the prisoners in the garage from which you had been taken?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. They would take them at night and beat them either in front of the door or upstairs in the corridor. Those people cried so much with pain that we were really worried. And the next day, it was Monday around 11.00, they brought in Major Dzaja. His head was bandaged so heavily that one couldn't see his eyes even, and they brought him in and then some people tried to tend to him and other people wanted to ask him questions. But then they said, "Well, don't. Don't you see what state he is in?" And we managed to put him on a couple of boards and covered him with a blanket and we left him like that for a while. The next morning they took out Vlatko --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Again, do you want us to deal with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might take the witness fairly quickly through this. You talk in paragraph 12 about a man named Vlatko Kapetanovic, you saw him, I believe, stuffed into the trunk of a black Mercedes and he was never seen alive again?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. They came early that morning. They took him. He was the half-naked one. They offered him a jacket because we were -- brought him from the cellar because it was cold, but then he subsequently found a T-shirt. They came to fetch him, took him out, and began beating him as soon as they got him out of the door. And through a cellar window I watched out, and there was a black Mercedes without any plates. They opened the boot and pushed him in. And inside, a man pulled me off that window so as not to watch because they had threatened us that whoever looked through the window would get beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You saw Mr. Kapetanovic stuffed into the trunk of this car with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, these prisoners that you talked about, sir, were any of them forced to perform manual labour?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, many were taken out by day. The first day, I believe, it was four or five of them, and they took them somewhere to load the looted goods or to bury somebody in a village. An incident happened that these people were attacked and beaten, and they returned or, rather, were brought back to the cellar badly beaten. When they moved them there, I heard that Mario was so badly beaten that he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, we're moving along here, and if you could keep your answers short, I'm sure that we would all appreciate that. You describe in paragraph 13 of your outline being taken from the monastery after about 10 days of captivity and then essentially herded through the town by armed Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, ten of us were taken out of the nunnery of the monastery. And one of them, who used to be my student, but he pretended not to know me, surprised me. And we were walked through the town and that was the first time I saw the town. I saw buildings destroyed. Muslim villagers were shouting in the streets, "Kill off the Ustashas," spit at us, and threw stones at us. But they took us through the town and into the cellar of the Bugojno secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I believe that you were detained there with about 40 other people in a small room?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. And in others, because there were a number of these cells and I could see that in other cells there were some other people, Croats, who had been detained. Some were civilians, some were policemen, and even two women were in a cell and I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then I believe you were taken to the sports hall of a local school, where you saw about 370 other detainees.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. I counted them, and believe that is an accurate figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What kind of provisions were provided to these 370 detainees? Could you give us an idea whether it was adequate food?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: At first they gave us nothing. Then the next day, between 6.00 and 7.00 in the afternoon, a Muslim soldier threw in some five or six loaves of bread, of mouldy bread, and a potful of -- a pot of stew. I mean, I think that this pot is about six or seven litres capacity -- and he simply pushed that through the door and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And was that typical of the provisions that were given to the prisoners during their captivity, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: They gave us no food while we were in the school, but Croats who were freer brought the food before the school and asked the guards. Some guards did not dare, but others did, and managed to give us that food on the sly. But otherwise we did not get any food.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that you were released on August 5th, 1993 and placed under house arrest.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Told to report to the police station on a daily basis. Did you do so?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I did not report, and I immediately went out into the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Why did you decline to report to the police station, as directed? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcript

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I thought it was degrading. I thought I should go to their official representatives and tell them that I would not do it and that I wanted to bring back to life the Croat side, I mean the party, and that is what I did subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You've previously stated that you became one of the de facto representatives, or a spokesman for the few remaining Croats in Bugojno. Tell us: I believe in mid-August of 1993 you visited a detention camp established at the soccer stadium in the town. Could you just describe for the Court how many people were kept there and whether you made any arrangements to help them.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Since they would not allow us to visit, I decided to test them, so I simply went there, had some food with me and some cigarettes that I could lay my hands on, because I wanted to see what was going on there. And they -- I simply went to the gate and they told me I had to apply to so-and-so, to their boss. But since I knew those Muslims who were there, I said, "Well, I have some mail, pieces of paper, and I have some food, and I want to give it to those men and to see them." And I could see those men through the grid. So I gave this food to those Muslims and then I saw how they distributed amongst themselves, that is, the prisoners, and never got it. But my purpose was to see what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How many people were kept prisoner in this soccer stadium, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Since I began to make some -- to keep some records, I and the group that I put together. There were some 600, then 500, because they released some, and the final figure is 542.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When was this camp disbanded or dissolved?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Only as late as 1994, 19th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And were any of the detainees -- did any of the detainees disappear, never to be heard from again; and if so, how many?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, 26 of them. Of those 26 have been traced, or rather their bodies, so 21 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: During the -- or immediately after the Muslim attack on Bugojno in mid-June of -- July of 1993, Mr. Mrso, could you just give us an estimate of how many Croat civilians were forced out of their homes and out of the municipality immediately?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: As this group was set up in order to take stock of the situation, I believe that of the Croat inhabitants of Bugojno, there are 2.700 to 3.000 Croats that stayed in Bugojno at that moment, after the attack. All the others fled, were expelled, and those were the figures that we used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know how many, approximately, were expelled, how many Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Between twelve and thirteen thousand were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You describe the two or three thousand Croat civilians who stayed behind in Bugojno following the Muslim attacks, sir. What was life like for the people that stayed behind?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Impossible. They plundered everything. When I left out, I learned why there was detention. It was because -- so they could loot the houses, so that many people fled through the woods, to just leave Bugojno. And when I set up the office every morning, they came to report to me, that is, whoever did, about various acts of brigandry, about harassment, about breaking into houses at night, about ransacking of the homes, about the search of houses in search of money and valuables. People were frightened and we had nothing, and we didn't even have anything to eat. Because even what we had, there was this tremendous pressure, because they would come and loot our houses time and again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not propose to ask any more questions about this. We would simply direct the Court to Exhibit D284/1 and to tabs 13 and 15, identified during the course of Lieutenant Colonel Gerritsen's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But Mr. Mrso, as a result of the incidents of harassment, plunder, looting and so forth that you have described, did any of the two or three thousand Croats who had been left behind after the Muslim attacks in July of 1993 leave Bugojno municipality?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. Many of them left. At some point there were only 900 or something like that left of us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So do you have an estimate of how many Croat civilians fled the municipality between July of 1993 and the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I think about 1.500, if not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And I believe, sir, that you discovered that your brother's house had been attacked by Muslim troops, ABiH troops. Could you just describe what you know of that event to the Court.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I was told this by a man who was there at the time of the capture. They were already breaking the front door and the garage of my brother's and taking the car away and taking out my brother, my mother, and my sister-in-law through the back door. My brother resisted, said, "My mother is ill. We have to help her." But they said, "No, no, no. You all must go," and they took them three streets away. And then a Muslim who, in all that fracas went to look for somebody, came upon the cellar of that house and saw the three of them killed, with yet another neighbour, Mico Grlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I believe that you've stated in your outline that the bodies of your relatives who were killed had never been found following their killing.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. I heard later on. It was said that they had killed the manager of Gorica. My brother was the director of the town planning institute in Bugojno. And somebody said that those bodies were collected -- I do not know whether it is true or not -- that they were put on a small -- in a small delivery van of yellow colour and driven away somewhere, but I do not know whether it is true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Just one question before I turn to my final subject, Mr. Mrso. I believe that you have actually been in conversations with the investigators for the Prosecution of this Tribunal and told them what you know about what happened to you and others in Bugojno during these terrible times.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, and we're still talking. And we have, yes, appointments made. Yes, I've spoken to them repeatedly. They requested a much more exhaustive account than you are asking me to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Thank you. Now, one of the arguments being made in this case by the Prosecution is that political leaders of the HDZ, BiH, amongst others, caused, planned, or instigated or ordered or committed or helped in the perpetration of a widespread and systematic campaign of persecution aimed deliberately against Bosnian Muslim civilians and that this was pursued throughout the territory of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, including in the municipality of Bugojno. Could you tell the Court, sir, what your reaction to that claim is? Is there any truth in it or not?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I think it was fabricated by institutions not like this one but similar, which are against Croats who have a different idea about Bosnia. I was involved in politics, albeit not at a very high level, but at the meetings that I attended I never heard anything like that being said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who harassed or persecuted whom in Bugojno, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, I can say that, I can prove that, I can corroborate it, I can document it: that not only then, there is still harassment by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Against whom?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Against whom are these acts of harassment being conducted?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Muslims are harassing Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You also make a reference in paragraph 19 of your statement, coming to the end of your testimony now, Mr. Mrso, at least on direct examination, about an agreement that had been reached only a week before the surprise attack launched upon Croats in Bugojno on the 18th of July, 1993. Could you tell us a little bit about that, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. And it was aired by the local radio and television, because there was no reason for mutual attacks, because the threat coming from the Serbs was evident. And those who took part in this could tell you that. I was not one of them, but I heard about it and I heard stories about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The agreement that you've said was announced on local radio and television, this was an agreement reached between Muslims and Croats not to fight one another but rather to direct their attentions towards the common Serb threat; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They even arranged a rather nice party on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The last set of questions I've got for you, sir, concern one of the two defendants in this case, one of the two accused, Mr. Kordic. Did he have any influence, as far as you could see, on the events in Bugojno prior to mid-1994?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I do not think he had any. I did not know Kordic. It was only later on that I met him, that I saw him at some meetings. And there was a warehouse in the territory of his municipality where we captured some food reserves, and that was when I established contact with him. That is, he asked the man who worked for him to establish the needs of his municipality so that when we began to distribute, he would know that. But I did not -- otherwise I did not know personally Mr. Kordic. And Mr. Blaskic, I never met him. I do not think he ever came to Bugojno during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you say you do not think he ever came to Bugojno during that time, do you mean Mr. Kordic or Mr. Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Kordic. Mr. Kordic. I do apologise. It was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just to make sure that the record is clear, sir: To your knowledge, at any time between the years 1991 and 1994, did Mr. Kordic visit your town, Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No. I claim that he did not, as far as I know. If he did, let him say so. But I came to know Mr. Kordic better, even insisted on his coming to Bugojno after the HDZ convention in late 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mrso. I'm Goran Mikulicic. I'm a lawyer from Zagreb representing the second accused, Mr. Mario Cerkez. We have not met before, we never talked or met, and I should therefore like to seize this opportunity to ask you only a few questions. Mr. Mrso, let us go back to the first half of 1992. You told us that in late May, or rather on the 24th of May, Bugojno was attacked by the JNA and the army of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Bugojno is adjacent to the municipality of Novi Travnik, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us that the HVO assumed upon itself the defence against this attack, whereas the Muslim forces kept rather aloof. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, the HVO units in Bugojno, were they helped, both in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcript sense of armament by the units from some other municipalities in Central Bosnia [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Mrso: You did routes of the villages. Did you visit the villages of Grbici [phoen] and Medina?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You did not go there?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, have you heard of the factory Slavkorodic?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Will you briefly tell us where is it and what did it manufacture at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: It is on the way from Bugojno to Kupres, above the village of Cipolici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What system is it?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what kind of a system it had, but I think that it was manufacturing parts for weapons or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina that factory was under JNA supervision?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And to stop beating about the bush, it made weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. I had some friends who worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And when the Croat Muslim broke out or rather when Muslims attacked Bugojno, who took over control over that factory?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, Serbs, by and large. According to my friends, and we discussed these matters, they immediately began to take away the explosives those -- what do you call them -- the fuses and these things. The Serbs simply took it and took it away. And then I told my friends, "Well, you do the same."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But after the attack of the Bosnian Serb army in the latter half of 1992 and former half of 1993, who was de facto in control of that factory, was it the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, and that is why I argued why don't they take it over because the Serbs kept it. And then when they fled, they looted it all and nobody had the control over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you mean there was no -- the manufacturing had stopped in the factory?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answers, Mr. Mrso, I -- that is all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, I have a few questions for you. Would it be correct to describe Bugojno as lying between Herzegovina and Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't know geographically whether it would be precise, but you could say so -- not immediately, because Tomislavgrad and Prozor municipalities are really the municipalities that border on Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But for the viability of Herceg-Bosna, was Bugojno really rather important because it linked Central Bosnia to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was essential. To me, it wasn't. To me, the important thing was for the Croats to be able to defend themselves against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were a party to the setting up of the party in your area, weren't you, of the HZ HB -- HDZ, rather, in your area, you were a party to that?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Not directly because it -- as manager, I was in Livno. I was working on bringing back a company in Livno, but I did join.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you must have appreciated at that stage that, given the ethnic distribution within your town, there was the risk that your party would cause upset amongst the other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't think that this is what should be put to me. It was not in terms of ethnicity that we considered things at that time, it was just to defend ourselves from the Chetnik aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but the -- I don't want to go through all the documents because we've looked at the general documents many times in this case already, but the documents establishing the party and then the documents establishing the HVO focus on Croats pretty well to the exclusion of all others, don't they?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't know about these documents. I was never in any meetings that discussed only Croats. We only discussed Bugojno, and those were all-inclusive discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as you were concerned, the HVO, when it was established, who had established it or what had established it?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't understand. What establishment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The HVO wasn't established by a popular vote or anything of that sort, was it?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't know about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was established by a political party, wasn't it? I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, could the witness repeat --

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't know who was in charge of its establishment. What we asked to be done was to establish a Crisis Staff so that the defence could be organised. I don't know at what level it was established. I was not a part of it and I don't know who was in charge. I don't know the establishing documents. I'm not an expert in these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've made some observations about whether Mr. Kordic ever visited Bugojno, but help me with this, in Bugojno, how did you understand the lines of communication and command to operate so far as the HVO or your party was concerned? Who did you look to for superior authority?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Since I was in the party, I was not in the HVO, I only learned about things in the party meetings. I did not ask who was in charge for the establishment or for communication. As a citizen, I was especially interested in the defence, and this is what we, in the party, were interested in and I guess the party leadership, at that time, did discuss that. At that time, I was not in the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you telling us that you simply don't know who, at the material time, outside Bugojno, was coordinating or leading the military activities in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I really do not know. Even now I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I shan't trouble with you that. But save for this, you accept, presumably, that wars are ultimately directed by politicians?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: If you say so. I, myself, will not go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that there is another version of events about Bugojno, and necessarily advanced by the Muslims and, in particular, by a man called Dzevad Mlaco?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: You are asking me, sir, but can you specify exactly what you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know the man Dzevad Mlaco. He was the former head of your municipality.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, I know him very well. We were in contact throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And is he a man who there's reason to doubt or is he a man against whom there are things we should maybe be careful about what he says?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, I also asked through the International Community members, I asked that I -- that Mr. Mlaco should be removed as the head of the municipality, and I said that I would leave and I would invite all the Croats to leave if Mr. Mlaco stayed on in the position of the head of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So your objections to him were what? So that we can understand how things are, what were your objections to him?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Because he was the president of the War Presidency in Bugojno, and he did everything he could to have Croats expelled from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. That reveals the contrary attitude of one to the other; I understand that. Is it right that there was, at some stage, a document created in 1992 in Bugojno where the HVO forbade Muslims or Bosniaks from moving, restricted their movement? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't remember the document. I am not aware of it. But I know that Muslims came to me to ask for permission to go to Croatia to visit their loved ones who were staying there, but I know that I, myself, needed such permits and I couldn't always get them myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that -- there was a requirement for passes and you were in a position to issue them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No. I, myself, had to go and request one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From the HVO would that be?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard about a meeting in Bugojno on the 15th of March of 1992 where the party leader, Kljuic, attended. Were you present at any part of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, I was not present. No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You mention the man Tole. Do you know very much about him?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No. Nothing apart from what I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. You don't know who appointed him to his position originally?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you accept that the Bugojno HVO was benefitting from arms supplied by Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: How do you mean, in terms of defence, benefitting the defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. You were being armed, in part, directly by Croatia.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't know the sources, but personally I asked if -- that more be supplied if possible, but I don't know where exactly it was coming from or who was supplying them, because I was not directly involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the Court's record, there is a document in the international armed conflict file, 2376.1, dated 11th of September, 1992 dealing with the supply of arms, and I needn't trouble this witness with it in light of what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Equally, were you aware of orders being sent to your municipality in October 1992 seeking identification of Croatian army officers who were working in your area and in your units at that time, because there were actually Croatian soldiers, it may be, in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, I don't know, sir. And again, let me repeat, I was not within the military structure. I was within the political structures in the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. But the political structures and the military structures were very closely connected, were they not?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: This is something that you can assert. I can only say what we discussed within the party, and when we discussed it, we did it on behalf of the party that the defence should be intensified, that it should be better organised. But in terms of military organisation, I don't know any details. I just had no access to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you press or call for further assistance from Croatia, and did you call for or press for Croatian soldiers to come and assist you?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Who, myself or someone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a politician, you were concerned about defence, did you do that?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, we never asked that. I personally thought that we had enough forces in Bugojno that we could do a lot on our own, that is, in cooperation with others in the municipality. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcript

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, again the document which deals with detailing Croatian officers in Bugojno is 2383. Perhaps the witness could look with us at Exhibit 249 very briefly. Perhaps I'll just give this to the usher and we can lay it on the ELMO and the witness can see the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the date here which is said to be October, 1992, how central were you to the leadership of your party or of your community?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Not very much. I was a member of the municipal board. I wasn't even in the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But were you kept informed of things that were going on as the position generally deteriorated?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I never heard of this and I've never seen it, but I got informed through daily meetings and to that extent, yes, I was informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you see, this is a document that reflects the movement of battalions from Bugojno in the direction of Ravno with the intention, it's said, of joining up with other Muslim forces. Can you remember any concern being expressed in October 1992 about the movement of such forces and the reinforcing of Muslim forces in the Ravno area?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I only know that the incidents had started in the part of the municipality towards Novi Travnik. But there are two roads: There is a road from Bugojno to Travnik and from Uskoplje to Gornji Vakuf. And this is not Ravno, this is Ravno Rostovo. That is on the Bugojno side and the Muslims kept the so-called illegal checkpoints and Croats were harassed and at -- I don't know about these troop movements, I hear this for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, what this document shows, it appears, is that if such units participated in fighting, there would be the use of artillery on Bugojno. Now, I wondered if that was something that was drawn to your attention at the time because it would be a matter of great concern.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Sir, I don't -- I am not following you very well. If this was the Muslim army going to Bugojno, that means that they were not going to defend against the Serbs. But if they were going towards Travnik, there were no Serbs there so I don't know what to conclude from what you are asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question that I'm asking you is whether you were aware at the time that the possibility of artillery being focussed on Bugojno and that would, of course, be on the Muslim sector of Bugojno. Do you remember that being a possibility at that time of 1992, 24th of October?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Whose artillery to go to Bugojno? Whose forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The HVO artillery focussed on the Muslim sector of Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well that is not true. That never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next document again that I needn't put to this witness, just for sequence, is 2392, which again deals with the provision of armaments for Bugojno from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if we then turn to 1993. By 1993, say, early spring, was it a state of cooperation between you and the Muslims or was there growing tension?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I think that misunderstandings and tensions kept escalating.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was one of the causes for the escalation the fact that the HVO was being armed and, perhaps, from time to time, being armed by Croatia so that it was gathering power and strength?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: That was not the reason, and from this distance, I can say that at that time, Muslims were already turning against Croats because they saw that the Serbs had taken half of the territory and they, I guess, wanted to take the other half for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, we've had a bit of evidence, it's at transcript page 6026 and the witness called Williams. We've had a bit of evidence about how some HVO artillery in March 1993 was left with its guns facing the Muslim sector of Bugojno. The suggestion that that particular witness made was that this was a pointer towards the Muslim sector of Bugojno being a possible HVO military target. Now, had things, by March 1993, deteriorated to such an extent that the HVO would have to be laying its guns in the direction of the Muslim sector of Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: It had been so things would not happen in Bugojno that the Muslims took it with -- and prepared that and I think that these -- this person came to so mistrust between Muslims and Croats in order to protect the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's probably the translation but I don't fully understand your answer. Are you accepting that by March 1993, the HVO might have been laying its guns in the direction of the Muslim sector of Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No. We wanted to protect ourselves from the Serbs. Had we thought otherwise, then we would not have lost Bugojno as we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's another document -- and again I needn't trouble you with it. It's 643 -- for April of 1993, which relates to having Croatian army units, officers, listed. Are you quite sure there wasn't a buildup of Croatian personnel in your area? This one, I think, is not specific to --

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, sir, because on one occasion I asked that a military expert be brought in. We in Bugojno did not know how to do these things, so I wish that we had gotten some people who would be able to lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That last document is not specific to Bugojno; it's general to several municipalities. The same man, Dzevad Mlaco, might say that at this period of time there were still joint institutions operating and functioning reasonably well; in particular, there was a joint police force. Would you accept that? This is just March and the spring of 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Can I accept, sir: The misunderstanding in Bugojno stems from the fact that the Muslims never accepted the election results, and no institution could function because of their obstruction. And so no institution can serve the citizens of Bugojno, and that's where all the misunderstanding stemmed from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say "the election results," you mean what?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: That the HDZ got the majority in the parliament and the Muslims in their leadership in Sarajevo obstructed and we never established any functioning institution as we agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there in fact a joint police force operating until indeed the 17th of July of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Formally, but not in the full sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In April of 1993, do we get a fair picture of the way things were organised by this: There was a document -- we can look at it if you'd like. It's 653.1. But we won't look at it immediately, to save time. There was a document whereby Valenta sent to the presidents of various communities, including yours, orders about curfews. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No. I don't know that the curfew was ever claimed or declared in Bugojno, and I was there at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't have that document to hand. I may or may not want to show it to the witness. I don't have many more questions, but I'd be grateful for the opportunity of just tidying up over the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We're going to adjourn now until half past 11.00. Mr. Mrso, don't speak to anybody about your evidence during the adjournment until it's over, and don't let anybody speak to you about it. Half past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just look briefly at this exhibit -- I'll hand this one in. Oh, there it is, coming up -- which is Exhibit 653.1. Mr. Mrso, we see that this is an order that went to various municipalities, including Bugojno, on the 14th of April of 1993, referring to intensified tensions following a number of incidents in the majority of municipalities. Then it orders a curfew to be imposed and the closing of catering establishments and the stopping of schools working. Do you remember this happening?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, I don't. I really don't. It never reached me. And even if that was so, I did not go by this. But this is of the 15th, not of the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, then. Maybe the translation is wrong. Indeed, it is. Thank you for drawing that to our attention. But is the reality that the assumption of power by the HVO in, for example, your community, was a cause of irritation, to put it at its lowest, to the Muslims who were there in slightly smaller numbers but nevertheless very substantial numbers originally?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I understand this question properly, we never took over the power in Bugojno, the HVO, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had you sought to do so?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll look at one more document before I come to the 17th of July, and although it's a military document, I'd nevertheless like your comments on it, please. It's 1085.1. While it's coming to you, what do you recollect in about June of 1993 as to have been the military activity of the Muslims and the military activity of the HVO in your area? Who was doing what?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, it was like this, if I remember: By that time, incidents had already escalated, and the circumstances were such that I thought it necessary to report to the leadership in Mostar, and I requested to be allowed to go out in order to inform that the situation was unsafe. However, the HVO representatives would not let us go. I wasn't alone. There were three of us. I nevertheless managed to go out and report. The Muslims had begun to seize vehicles, to attack civilians, as I have already told you, setting up checkpoints at all sorts of places, including corners of streets in the town, and I realised that something was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that, if I may, a little later. The question maybe wasn't properly asked. But forgetting incidents that were causes of unhappiness between Muslims and Croats in your town, who -- on a wider scale, who was fighting whom? Were the Croats fighting the Serbs? Were the Muslims fighting the Serbs? What was the position?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: It was like this: We focused on the defence against Serbs, because that is where we perceived the danger, and insisting that regardless of misunderstandings, we should go together with Muslims and reinforce the defence. Because we have already heard about what had happened at Kupres: Information was arriving, the town was under constant shelling, one could barely go out anywhere, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And are you telling us, then, that there was still active warfare between the Croats and the Serbs in the late spring/early summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. The combatants were on the front lines. I even went out to visit them in the direction of Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And there had been no change in the relations between Serbs and Croats, of which you were aware, for example, following the agreement in Graz?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I haven't the foggiest. One did not feel that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at this document, which is the 20th of June of 1993, and is a Military Intelligence Service report coming from the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade. And there's just a couple bits of it that I'd like to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcript draw to your attention and ask your comment on. It speaks of the area of Prusac, which is a little what, north-west of Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: It is a village which is in the Donji Vakuf municipality, down the road from Bugojno to Donji Vakuf to the left; however, off the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Quite close by?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Towards Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Quite close by?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it says of the Muslims that the MOS has one -- well, if you start at the top, it says: "This sector comprises the village of ..." and it sets the villages out. It says that the Muslim armed forces has about 1.200 men under arms in total. And for Prusac, it says that they have one reinforced battalion of about 400 soldiers. The area is well fortified in the engineering sense, and all artillery pieces in the area are used for defence against Chetniks. Then it says this: "According to our information, in the case of a conflict between the HVO and the MOS, there should be no major disengagement of enemy forces from this area. Prusac battalion had priority in the distribution of material and technical equipment over the other units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and now has, in addition to infantry weapons, and then it lists them, [indiscernible] positioned in Prusac." So that's one passage I'd like you to help us with. And then if we go to Guvna, we see what's said there about the men. And if we, in the English version, go over to the page, it then says that should a conflict break out, it may be that some of these weapons would be disengaged and transferred in the direction of Porice. So one thing is quite clear, that the Muslims were actively engaged at the front line; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: In this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may not be clear from this document, but are you saying that the HVO were also, themselves, in these same areas actively defending against the Serbs or was it being left to the --

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes -- no. First, they were primarily Croat positions because Guvna is a mixed village, Muslims and Croats. And the first village which Chetniks attacked from Donji Vakuf was Guvna, and they went to that village the next day to see, and some houses and some cow shacks had already been put on fire, and there were shell fragments which I took with me to Bugojno. But I could not agree about it and I know one occasion and I am not sure that I am right, but a gentleman from Bugojno could confirm this that they were in talking that HVO would help them around Prusac. That is what I know about it. I think that was the only stronghold because Prusac, as I have said, is a Donji Vakuf village. It means a great deal to Muslims so that that is where they had some noteworthy forces and strongholds. They were not as present on other front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Your Honour will just give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Under the Prusac heading, we see in the translation, and I trust in the original, that it says, "In the case of a conflict between the HVO and the MOS, there should be no major disengagement of enemy forces from this area." What would enemy relate to there, the word "enemy"?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. Perhaps they mean Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or perhaps they mean the Muslims, do you mean, because that's my question. Looking at the two references here to the possibility of a conflict breaking out, were the Muslims already being regarded as the enemy by June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't think so. This is how I see it: I think it is correct that from the beginning, Serbs have been trying -- not with us -- Serbs were trying to negotiate with the municipality in order to pass through Rama and Prozor. And at party meetings, we were asking the head not to talk to Serbs anymore, not to receive them because we feared that Serbs would use the troops to link with their forces towards Konjic, Mostar, and I think this is what this text was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there any question, do you think, looking back, of the HVO stirring up trouble and looking for a fight with the Muslims at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Sir, if you are talking trouble that the Croats undertook, the defence of Bugojno against Chetniks, that's one matter. And another matter, I do not know that anybody complained to me when -- anybody complained to me that somebody had been beaten or harassed or anything. I still live with those people there. You keep asking me questions that I must take a reserved stand towards, because I was with the civilian arm of the HVO, not the military one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then let's move to the 17th, not the 18th of July. You tell us that, in answer to a question of mine, that there was a joint police force formally. What do you mean by "formally"?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, the Muslims never agreed about the power distribution to have the head of police a Croat and the head of municipality which had been agreed, because as a party which won the elections, they were entitled to it but they would never agree to that, and that was the root of all the misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the joint police force existed and operated, and I must ask you: Was it perhaps the HVO and your side that was treating it as a formality and not taking, say, the joint police force as seriously as it might have been taken?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: It couldn't because it believed that the executives who came from the -- which -- who had been appointed by the Croat side but that was the result of the political negotiations and the result of the elections, and the Muslims would not comply with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it right that on the 17th of July, that's one day before the breakup that you speak of, joint police patrols of Croats and Bosniaks were, in fact, arrested by the HVO and at the same time, is it right, that Bosniak civilians were being arrested on that day, the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: That is not true. On the 17th of July, Muslims killed a Croat soldier standing on guard in a village where Croats had organised it. And on the 17th, he was buried and I attend it personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be, but that's not the issue. Were there arrests of Muslim civilians on the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, as we move on to the 18th, I couldn't help but note that when you were asked about the 18th, asked who attacked whom you replied, "From what I know now," and you have obviously constructed your answer from what you have learned since. At the time it was entirely unclear, wasn't it, I suggest, who started the conflict?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: It was clear, sir. That afternoon I told you, between 7.00 and 8.00, Muslim soldiers already began to break into Croat homes, expel Croats, loot and so on and so forth. And then in the night between the 18th and 19th, a Muslim came to my door requesting to open, I guess, in order to kill me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We don't need to go through that again, not because I'm not sympathetic about it but because we've covered it once. Can you tell us, please, about the use made by the HVO of the Akvarijum motel.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, do you know a place called the Akvarijum hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it right that that hotel or -- that perhaps its grounds rather than the hotel itself, I can't put this to you, but is it right that that hotel was the location of an HVO camp where people were detained?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't know, believe me. Because of the shelling, there was so much of it then that it never crossed my mind to go to that motel or anything. I never even heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you aware that the man Dzevad Mlaco said that it was used as a camp, and a large number of Bosniaks were taken from there and killed on the 18th of July. 45, I think, is the number he puts on it.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: It is not true. That is absolutely not true, sir. I would have known if a single Muslim had been killed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One of our witnesses, a recent witness, has told the Chamber that Bugojno was the mirror image in many ways and for some period of time with the town of Prozor where, in each place, the ethnic distributions were reversed, and what was happening in one place by one group was happening in the other place but being done by the other group. Do you know enough about Prozor to accept, in general terms, that that description from Mr. Gerritsen a couple of weeks ago, was correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I do not know enough about that, but I know -- I mean I learned later that the Muslim, or rather the Muslim policy, was to open the road to Sarajevo/Mostar, and they were planning to, among other things, take Prozor. Whether this is correct or not, I don't know. I learned that subsequently from contacts with people from Prozor, and they reportedly have some documents to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last document and simply one that I put to you for completeness because it's something that you said to one of the international observers is 1242.2. But while it's coming to you, can you help us at all, in general, with how it is or at least how it appears to be the position that the account of Bugojno's suffering that you give doesn't find its way into reports of either European monitors very much or the military at the time. Can you explain that to us? We don't seem to have many documents setting out, contemporaneously, the account that you've given to the Chamber. Can you give an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: When I see the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no, before we come to this document which is a little later. Let me ask the question another way: Were you seeing monitors and international military peacekeepers in the course of July and August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: In July, not even in theory. In August, likewise, because I had just left the camp. Perhaps end of August or later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And to which -- did you or did other people in your presence give accounts of what had happened to some of the international observers and if so, can you tell us to whom so we can just track it down and check it? That's all.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: We told people. I don't know exactly the date when the representatives of the International Red Cross came and those ECMM, UNPROFOR, it's then representative, the English UNPROFOR and those people did not sympathise with us. I believe they concealed their reports deliberately and I know we read those reports and tried to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you have any evidence for that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, what proof? Perhaps if you ask me a direct question, I just might have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I asked a direct question. Do you have any evidence for your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: From that period or directly at the time which the gentleman mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, just to pick up His Honour's concern and the question I want, I was asking you about really the accounts that you might have given to people in, say, September of 1993 and I think you were answering that the English UNPROFOR didn't sympathise and you think they concealed their reports. Can you help me at all with which international observers you spoke to at the time? Was it monitors or was it British UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I'd have to look it up in my diary. I did not say that these people hid these documents.
